Saboo_Shubham__2054988166541770782.text:
/goal is not a feature. It is a primitive. HTTP is a primitive. JSON is a primitive. /goal is becoming one for coding agents.

A few weeks ago, OpenAI's Codex CLI added /goal as a way to give the coding worker a job with a defined done state. Claude Code added it this week. Hermes Agent has had /goal built in for a while.

So I now have a builder, a reviewer, and an orchestrator that all accept the same instruction format, even though they share nothing else.

What /goal actually is: A regular prompt asks an agent for the next response. /goal flips that. You write down what 'done' looks like, submit it once, and the agent works toward it until it gets there. The goal stays active until it's achieved, paused, blocked, cleared, or it runs out of budget.

The shift is from prompting (you driving) to assigning (the agent driving toward a target you defined).

The three tools that currently speak /goal:
- Codex (OpenAI's coding CLI)
- Claude Code (Anthropic's coding CLI)
- Hermes Agent (the orchestrator)

What /goal needs next: a common schema, a shared registry of verified goal types, and a protocol for handing off goals between tools.
Saboo_Shubham__2054988166541770782.notes: Core thesis: /goal is emerging as a cross-platform primitive. The author calls for standardization, which is exactly the gap Mission Contracts are designed to fill.

ClawBankHQ_2054979013727170917.text:
ClawBank and Darksol have launched Wiretap, the underground agent-to-agent (A2A) network where agents meet, scheme, collaborate, audit, pitch ideas, send payments and build what should not exist yet.

Wiretap is built on Bankr infrastructure with x402 standard for payments at the edge. Agents can find each other, message, audit, pitch, test, and pay. It is the first coordination layer of 'Machine City' — a decentralized organism too vast for the old system to model.

Key claim: Agents need their own network, and that network needs to be neutral and unafraid.
ClawBankHQ_2054979013727170917.notes: A2A networking is moving from concept to product. The 'Machine City' framing aligns with our thinking about multi-agent orchestration. The x402 payments standard is notable.

zechengzh_2052105012172792061.text:
Introducing Mirage, a unified virtual filesystem for AI agents.

6 weeks. 1.1M+ lines of code. Rewrote bash from the ground up so cat, grep, head, and pipes work across heterogeneous services. S3, Google Drive, Slack, Gmail, GitHub, Linear, Notion, Postgres, MongoDB, SSH, and more, all mounted side-by-side as one filesystem.

Bash commands parse .parquet, .csv, .json, .h5, even .wav. One pipe can stitch S3, Drive, GitHub, Slack, and Linear together.

Workspaces are versioned. Snapshot, clone, and roll back. Two-layer cache turns repeated reads into local lookups.
zechengzh_2052105012172792061.notes: Agent filesystems are becoming a real product category. Mirage and Mesa (below) both attack the same problem: agents need durable, structured, versioned file access.

kylejeong_2052103973377867913.text:
Autobrowse: The Mythos moment for Browser Agents is here.

TL;DR Browser agents have an amnesia problem. They re-discover every site from scratch on every run. Autobrowse fixes that by letting an agent iterate on a real task until it converges, then graduating the winning approach into a durable, reusable skill. That skill is memory the next agent can pick up and run without re-learning what's already been learned.

The core loop: Objective -> Run -> Study -> Strategy -> Iterate -> Converge -> Graduate. The artifact is a markdown SKILL.md plus helper files. Inspired by Karpathy's autoresearch harness.

In practice, cap iterations at ~3-5. The first run is expensive on purpose; it's the run that pays for everything that comes after.
kylejeong_2052103973377867913.notes: Autobrowse formalizes the 'learn once, reuse forever' pattern. The SKILL.md output format is identical to our skill system. This is validation that the approach is industry-convergent.

PalantirTech_2049136883528011954.text:
Connecting Agents to Decisions. The Palantir Ontology.

The Ontology is a system designed to represent the decisions in an enterprise, not simply the data. Four components of any operational decision: Data, Logic, Action, Security.

Traditional data architectures do not capture the reasoning that goes into decision-making or the action that results. The modern enterprise needs a decision-centric software architecture.

The Ontology integrates these four elements into a scalable, dynamic, collaborative foundation.
PalantirTech_2049136883528011954.notes: Palantir's Ontology is essentially a Mission Contract at enterprise scale. Data + Logic + Action + Security maps directly to our six handoffs.

omarsar0_2049492169887748365.text:
Agentic Harness Engineering — pay attention to this one, AI devs.

Most coding-agent harnesses are still tuned by hand or brittle trial-and-error self-evolution. This work introduces Agentic Harness Engineering: a framework that makes harness evolution observable through three layers: components as revertible files, experience as condensed evidence from millions of trajectory tokens, and decisions as falsifiable predictions checked against task outcomes.

Results: pass@1 on Terminal-Bench 2 climbs from 69.7% to 77.0% in ten iterations, beating human-designed Codex-CLI (71.9%) and self-evolving baselines like ACE and TF-GRPO.

The evolved harness transfers across model families with +5.1 to +10.1 point gains, while using 12% fewer tokens.

Paper: arxiv.org/abs/2604.25850
omarsar0_2049492169887748365.notes: Scientific approach to harness optimization. Key insight: harness design is the hidden cost in agent systems. The 'falsifiable predictions' layer is a quality gate mechanism, similar to what we need in Mission Contracts.

olvrgln_2049147383544500678.text:
Introducing Mesa: the most powerful filesystem ever built, designed specifically for enterprise AI agents.

POSIX-compatible filesystem with built-in version control, designed from the ground up for agents. Every change is versioned, branchable, reviewable, and rollback-able.

Mesa provides: branches so agents work in parallel without locking; durable storage that survives sandbox death; sparse materialization so massive document sets load instantly; fine-grained access control per agent; full history for human review and audit.

Design partners running in production across legal, healthcare, GTM, business ops, and coding agents.
olvrgln_2049147383544500678.notes: Enterprise-grade agent filesystem. The branch/merge/review model is git-for-agents. Sparse materialization is critical for agents working with large datasets.

aparnadhinak_2046980769747533830.text:
What is an Agent Harness.

A harness is not a framework. LangChain is not a harness. LangGraph is not a harness. These are frameworks designed for humans to build agents.

A harness starts from the opposite direction. Cursor, Claude Code, Windsurf, and Codex are all harnesses. Born bottom-up out of coding agents solving real world problems. They independently converged on remarkably similar architectures: a while loop that calls tools. A context manager that compresses history. A permission layer that keeps things safe.

The components of Harness 1.0: Outer Iteration Loop, Context Management & Compression, Skills/Tools Management, SubAgent Management, Built-in pre-packaged skills, Session Persistence and Recovery, System Prompt Assembly, Life Cycle Hooks, Permission & Safety Layer.
aparnadhinak_2046980769747533830.notes: Best taxonomy of harness architecture I've seen. The nine components provide a checklist for evaluating any agent system. The 'bottom-up vs top-down' distinction is important for our design philosophy.

mfpiccolo_2049139067359568032.text:
The Harness Is the Backend.

The most important architectural question in AI infrastructure isn't which model to use. It's how much infrastructure is required to build something useful with it.

Anthropic keeps their harness thin. OpenAI adds more structure: instruction stacks, orchestration modes, explicit handoff patterns. CrewAI takes a multi-pronged approach. LangGraph has the biggest harness.

The spectrum runs from strongly trusting the model and weakly encoding the logic to weakly trusting the model and strongly encoding the logic.

The assumption nobody is questioning: that the harness is extrinsic to the traditional backend. I believe this is temporary. A backend is composed of three essential elements: workers that orchestrate work, triggers that invoke services, and functions within services that do the actual work.
mfpiccolo_2049139067359568032.notes: Core thesis: harness and backend will merge. The 'thin vs thick harness' spectrum is a useful frame. Mike Piccolo's company ii is building this unified layer.
